case.case_title: Brigadier Liyanage v. Chandrananda de Silva Secretary, Ministry of Defence and Others
case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. Application 506/99 (F.R.), decided on 2 November 1999

clause.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the failure to promote the petitioner to the rank of Major General violated his fundamental rights under Article 12(1) of the Constitution by being unreasonable, arbitrary, and discriminatory.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner argued that the failure to promote him was unreasonable, arbitrary, and capricious, violating his fundamental rights guaranteed by Article 12(1) of the Constitution, especially since he was acquitted and had an outstanding career record.
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the promotion was denied because it was not in the best interest of the Army, based on Regulation 12 of the Army Officers' Service Regulations, due to the petitioner's alleged failure to exercise due control over subordinates involved in the Embilipitiya disappearances case.
key_facts: The petitioner was suspended pending trial in the Embilipitiya disappearances case and was acquitted.
After acquittal, the Army Commander recommended the petitioner’s promotion to Major General.
Two other officers who superseded the petitioner were promoted to Major General.
The petitioner was not promoted on the ground that it was not in the best interest of the Army.
Other officers above and below the petitioner in the chain of command, including some indicted, were promoted.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The court interpreted Article 12(1) as guaranteeing equality before the law and equal protection, meaning the petitioner should not be treated differently without rational basis. The court found the failure to promote the petitioner was unreasonable, irrational, arbitrary, and capricious, violating Article 12(1).
reasoning.application_to_facts: The petitioner was acquitted and had an outstanding service record. Others in similar or worse positions, including those indicted, were promoted. The respondents failed to provide a rational basis for singling out the petitioner, making the denial of promotion discriminatory and violative of Article 12(1).
principles_established: Equal treatment in promotion decisions is required under Article 12(1).
Promotion decisions must be reasonable and not arbitrary or capricious.
Acquittal in criminal proceedings removes negative presumptions affecting promotion.
Failure to provide rational explanation for differential treatment violates fundamental rights.

outcome.holding: The court held that the failure to promote the petitioner to Major General was a violation of his fundamental rights under Article 12(1) of the Constitution and ordered the implementation of the Army Commander's recommendation for promotion along with compensation and costs.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: The recommendations of the Commander of the Army dated 8th March 1999 to promote the petitioner were ordered to be implemented. The State was ordered to pay Rs. 50,000 as compensation and Rs. 5,000 as costs.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 12(1) was central to the court's reasoning as it guarantees equality before the law and equal protection, which the petitioner was denied by the arbitrary and unreasonable failure to promote him despite acquittal and comparable treatment of others.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The court found the failure to promote the petitioner was unreasonable, irrational, arbitrary and capricious and in the circumstances was violative of the petitioner's fundamental rights guaranteed by Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
